---
title: "Choosing a topic worth pursuing"
last-reviewed: "2026-09-06"
---

Before you commit to a topic, check whether you can get the data, recruit enough people and find the expertise you need. Search for studies that might already have answered the question.

These checks are often called due diligence. You can do many of them with a short search, a sample file or a conversation with the right person. Finding a problem now leaves you more room to change the project.

## Test the fragile assumptions first

Start with the assumption that would cause the most rework if it proved wrong. If the study depends on a restricted dataset, check access before refining the analysis. If it needs equipment you've never used, arrange a trial before committing to a collection schedule.

## What to check before committing {#the-due-diligence-domains}

### Importance and contribution

What problem is addressed, who cares, what present limitation matters and what bounded contribution could the evidence support?

### Prior evidence

Find what has been tried and where results conflict. Note the assumptions, measures, datasets and populations that dominate the evidence, along with any credible contrary findings.

### Question and inference

Check that the question can be answered with evidence you can obtain. Remove promises about causation, prevalence, representation, prediction or transfer that the proposed design cannot support.

### Access and recruitment

Identify who controls the participants, sites, archives, data, equipment or community relationships. Ask someone with authority to document access, then estimate plausible response, exclusion, attrition and downtime.

### Method and capability

Which designs are credible, what expertise is required, and can the team obtain it in time? Familiar software is not a methodological rationale.

### Ethics, governance and relationships

List the approval, consent, privacy, cultural governance, safety, partner and legal processes that apply. Record who decides, how long the process may take and which obligations continue after approval.

### Resources and time

Include training, licences, equipment, transcription, travel, participant reimbursement, storage, specialist review, analysis, reporting, correction and failure recovery.

### Dependencies and alternatives

Identify the assumptions that could stop the project. Develop a smaller, safer or more accessible route to the same problem before you need it.

::: {.decision-card}
**Smallest useful next action:** Complete the [Topic due-diligence canvas](../../templates/topic-due-diligence.qmd) using evidence rather than aspirations. Mark every unsupported statement as an assumption with an owner and test date.
:::

## Test assumptions cheaply

Before major commitment:

- ask the authoritative data owner what can actually be shared;
- estimate the eligible recruitment pool and plausible response;
- inspect a sample of the archive or dataset where permitted;
- trial the equipment or workflow with non-research material;
- seek specialist review of the central method;
- map approval lead times from current sources;
- test whether the core analysis is possible with simulated or public data;
- conduct appropriate consultation where communities or partners share authority.

For each test, decide in advance what result would let you continue and what would make you revise or stop. That gives the test a useful endpoint.

## Example: the prestigious but inaccessible dataset

A project proposes a novel analysis of a national administrative dataset. The proposal assumes access within six months.

Due diligence finds:

- applications are considered only twice each year;
- variables needed for the primary inference may not be released;
- analysis must occur in a secure environment;
- the student lacks one required method;
- a public dataset can address a narrower but related question.

The decision is not simply “wait for access”. The team records two designs, applies for controlled access, begins the required training and sets a gate: if variable availability is not confirmed by the stated date, the public-data question becomes the primary study.

## Decide how much checking is enough

| Finding | Response |
|---|---|
| Important, aligned and feasible | Proceed with documented assumptions and review triggers |
| Important but too broad | Narrow the population, claim, mechanism, period or number of studies |
| Important but one dependency is uncertain | Run a bounded feasibility test and preserve an alternative |
| Feasible but contribution is weak | Reframe the problem or stop before sunk costs grow |
| Approval or safety path is unclear | Pause affected work and seek responsible specialist guidance |
| Central evidence cannot support intended inference | Redesign or change the question |
| Stakeholder or community framing is not legitimate | Reopen problem definition and governance |

## How enthusiasm hides avoidable risk

Check the whole sequence as well as individual tasks. Recruitment, equipment and partner delays can overlap, and ethics approval may leave separate access or site permissions unresolved. Budget time for things going wrong.

Available data still need to fit the question. Familiar methods still need a rationale. Reconsider the project if those checks fail, even when you've already invested time in it.

## Run these checks before committing

Use the full [Before committing to each study](../../checklists/before-study-commitment.qmd) check. At minimum:

- [ ] importance, question, evidence and contribution align;
- [ ] critical access and resource claims are verified with responsible people;
- [ ] method and capability gaps have credible solutions;
- [ ] approval, cultural governance, safety and privacy paths are known;
- [ ] time and cost include failure scenarios;
- [ ] the main dependency has a continue, revise and stop rule;
- [ ] a realistic alternative has been considered;
- [ ] the decision and assumptions are recorded.

## Take the main uncertainty to supervision {#bring-evidence-for-the-go-or-change-decision}

Bring the one-page topic case, completed canvas, strongest contrary evidence, main dependency, one alternative and your recommendation. Ask which assumption would most damage the project if wrong and how cheaply it can be tested.

## Escalate or seek specialist input when

Access, ethics, privacy, safety, cultural governance, legal obligations, specialist methods, intellectual property, funding or partner authority exceeds the team's competence or decision rights.
